entry.title: London - Stroll along the South Bank

link.title: London - Stroll along the South Bank

entry.content:
When in London, I like to walk along the South Bank. It started by accident on my first visit in 2015, and I missed a lot of spots. I’d like to repeat the walk, add new places, and spend more time there whenever I get the chance.

I like to start at Waterloo Station, find the river, and keep it on my left all the way to Tower Bridge. That is the whole plan. No tickets to book, nothing to queue for unless I want to. It is a few kilometers of London at walking pace.

I have created a simple virtual walk for you to try: turn it, tip it, and fly the walk from stop to stop, with the landmarks named as you pass.

The Walk

  1. Waterloo Station. Where it starts. Step out of the station and follow the signs to the river.
  2. Southbank Centre. The Royal Festival Hall, from the 1951 Festival of Britain, and the skaters in the Undercroft.
  3. BFI Southbank. The cinema, and the second-hand book tables under Waterloo Bridge.
  4. National Theatre. Concrete terraces that people either love or hate.
  5. Gabriel’s Wharf. A little cluster of shops and cafés right on the river.
  6. Oxo Tower Wharf. Look up for the O, X, and O in the tower’s windows.
  7. Tate Modern. The old Bankside Power Station, an art gallery since 2000.
  8. Millennium Bridge. St Paul’s Cathedral, straight across the river.
  9. Shakespeare’s Globe. The theater, rebuilt close to where the original stood.
  10. Golden Hinde. A full-size replica of Sir Francis Drake’s ship.
  11. Southwark Cathedral. One of the oldest churches in London.
  12. Borough Market. Come hungry.
  13. HMS Belfast. A Second World War cruiser, moored for good.
  14. Tower Bridge. The one everyone pictures. Walk across, or just stand and look.
  15. Shad Thames. Old warehouses, cobbles, and walkways overhead. The end of the walk.

The Way Back

Or keep going: across Tower Bridge, and back along the north bank to where it started.

  1. Tower of London. Nearly a thousand years old, and a fortress, a palace, and a prison in its time.
  2. The Monument. Christopher Wren’s column to the Great Fire of 1666.
  3. St Paul’s Cathedral. Up Peter’s Hill from the river, with the dome at the end of the street.
  4. Somerset House. A courtyard that becomes an ice rink in winter.
  5. Cleopatra’s Needle. An Egyptian obelisk, about 3,500 years old. It has nothing to do with Cleopatra.
  6. Big Ben. The clock tower of the Houses of Parliament. Cross Westminster Bridge here.
  7. London Eye. Waterloo Station is a few minutes away, and the loop is closed.
entry.summary: When in London, I like to walk along the South Bank. It started by accident on my first visit in 2015, and I missed a lot of spots. I’d like to repeat the walk, add new places, and spend more time there whenever I get the chance.

entry.title: Emacs - the Start of a Journey

link.title: Emacs - the Start of a Journey

entry.content:
A Work-in-Progress.

Every editor I have used has held a version of me. The one who typed HTML by hand, the one who learned to build for the web, the one who wrote code for a living, and the one who now writes mostly words. Today, I am picking the editor that I hope will hold the rest of them.

I started all the way back with HotDog from Sausage Software, when making a web page felt like magic and the editor was the wand. Then came the humble Windows Notepad, which taught me that you need nothing more than a blank page and patience. TextPad came next, and I cared about it enough to write syntax files for it. BBEdit, when I moved to the Mac and never looked back. Coda, which made the web feel like one well-designed room. And then, in 2008, Sublime Text, which has been home ever since. I have been a loyal, paying customer from the first year, and I have happily paid for every upgrade since, hoping that it helps the people who make it keep making it. Each one of them was the right editor at the right time, and I remember each one fondly, the way you remember the houses you grew up in.

For a few years now, I have been quietly looking for an editor, an IDE1, to retire into. Something that will outlive trends, companies, and licenses. Something I can carry, unchanged, from one machine to the next for the rest of my life. Every time I looked, the final contenders were the same two, as they have been for decades: Vim and Emacs.

When I wrote about Sublime Text, I admitted that I was too lazy to learn either, and that I would probably end up with Vim. Well, I was wrong on both counts. Today, I have decided to give it time, go slow, and take the long journey with Emacs.

The Holy War

I would be lying if I said the choice did not come with a little guilt. Vim and Emacs users have been at it since the 1980s, in what is fondly called the editor war, and it is one of the few wars where nobody has ever lost anything except an afternoon.

The Vim camp likes to say that Emacs is a great operating system, lacking only a decent editor. The Emacs camp replies that Vim users are simply people who have not yet figured out how to quit. Emacs users are accused of having pinkies worn out from holding Control; Vim users are accused of being unable to type a sentence without first pressing Escape, just in case. Richard Stallman even appears, in robe and halo, as Saint IGNUcius of the Church of Emacs, who once declared that using a free version of vi is not a sin but a penance.

I am not picking a camp. I have the utmost respect for both, and for everyone who has spent a lifetime in either. I am only picking a home.

Slow and Minimal

I am not going to install a starter kit, nor copy someone else’s configuration of a thousand lines. I am staying minimal, as little as possible, and I will add to it only when I genuinely miss something. Every line in my configuration should be one I understand and can explain to myself a year from now.

The keyboard shortcuts will take time, and I am fine with that. I want them to settle into my fingers the way the alphabet did, one chord at a time, until I stop thinking about them. No rush. A shortcut learned slowly is one that stays.

My configuration lives with the rest of my dotfiles, and you are welcome to look. It is small, and I hope it stays that way.

Start with the Cards

If you are starting too, here is the one piece of advice I would give. Emacs comes with its own reference cards, as PDFs, inside the installation itself: the Survival Card for the first few days, and the Reference Card for everything after.2 Start there, not with a video or a blog post.

I printed and laminated mine. One stays at home, one at work, and one travels with me. There is something old-fashioned and right about learning a fifty-year-old editor from a card you can hold in your hand.

The Journey

I do not know where this goes. Perhaps in a few years Emacs will be where I write everything, these words included. Perhaps I will come back to this page and laugh at how little I knew. Either way, I will come back to it, and I will update it as I go.

This feels less like switching tools and more like coming home to something I always knew was there.

  1. An Integrated Development Environment, or IDE, is the one program where you write, run, and fix your code, instead of juggling a separate editor, compiler, and debugger. Emacs is, strictly, a text editor, but with the right packages it becomes as much of an IDE as you want it to be, and then some. ↩

  2. Both cards ship with Emacs as PDFs, in its etc/refcards/ folder, as survival.pdf and refcard.pdf, with translations alongside. On a Mac, they are inside the application, at /Applications/Emacs.app/Contents/Resources/etc/refcards/. From within Emacs, C-h v data-directory shows where that etc/ folder is on any machine. The GNU website also keeps them, at gnu.org/software/emacs/refcards. ↩

entry.title: Essentialism
entry.content:
I read Greg McKeown’s Essentialism in 2022, and like most good books, it said out loud what I had been slowly doing anyway. Less, but better.1 Over the years, I have applied it to what I own, and lately, more to the technology I live with.

This is my working list. It is not a system, and it will keep changing.

Native, and open formats. I prefer native apps over web apps dressed up as apps, and files over databases I cannot see. If my notes, photos, and writing are in plain text, Markdown, JPEG, or PDF, I can open them in twenty years with whatever exists then. A format I can walk away with matters more to me than a feature I will use twice.

Fewer accounts. I have been stepping away from online accounts that mean nothing to me,2 the ones I signed up for to try something once, or because everyone was. I no longer need to be an early user. If something is good, it will still be there in a year, and I will hear about it from someone I trust.

Essential apps only. My phone and my computer each have a short list of apps I actually use. Everything else goes. If I need it again, I can install it again; that has rarely happened. Not everything needs an app anyway.

Fewer subscriptions. Every subscription is a small promise to keep paying attention. I have canceled most of them. The ones that stay are the ones I would pay for again, today, without thinking.

Cables, without guilt. I used to keep every cable and adapter “just in case.” Now I want to be able to walk away from them, without the guilt, and without that dreaded nostalgia of the drawer. If a cable has not been used in a year, someone else can have it.

A dumb home. Our home setup is simple, and mostly dumb, on purpose. A switch should switch, and a lock should lock. Automation is an optional layer on top, and it is OK if it does not work. Nothing in the house should stop working because a server somewhere did.

Layers, like an onion. I think of everything in layers.3 The core is plain and must always work. Each layer on top adds convenience, and each one can be peeled away without breaking the one beneath it. That is how I dress, and that is how I want my technology to be.

Hobbies I can walk out of. I still tinker, build, and try things, and I enjoy it. The rule is that I should be able to walk out of any of it, any day, and nothing important falls apart.

No regrets. If I die tomorrow, I would like the family not to inherit a puzzle. No accounts to untangle, no subscriptions quietly charging, no closet of mystery boxes. Just a few good things, in their places, with backups, that anyone can understand.

References and Inspiration

  • Making quieter technology
  • Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less, Greg McKeown

  1. “Less, but better” is Dieter Rams’ Weniger, aber besser, the line he lived his design by at Braun. McKeown borrows it as the motto of the book. ↩

  2. Every account is one more place for my data to leak from. I would rather assume it will, and keep fewer of them. ↩

  3. I first wrote about the onion layers for security and privacy, where it is better known as defense in depth. The same thinking works for almost everything else. ↩

entry.title: Syntactic Sugar
entry.content:
Peter Landin coined the term syntactic sugar in 1964, in the paper, “The Mechanical Evaluation of Expressions.”1

In the world of programming languages, a[i] is sugar for *(a + i). A for loop is sugar over a jump and a counter. A class in JavaScript is sugar over prototypes. async and await are sugar over a state machine someone used to write by hand. In every case a compiler will show you the expansion which we do not have to look into. It makes life easier for all of us.

We’re now in world where AI commoditizes knowledge, nearly everything above the machine has turned into syntactic sugar, and we are left with having to get down to first principles. However, we need to be careful with it, because “just sugar” is the same dismissal people aim at design when they mean decoration. Syntax is a user interface for thought. Ken Iverson built a Turing Award lecture around that in 1979, calling notation a tool of thought. Sugar is the part made for humans.

English is, perhaps, now the top layer of syntax, and it is the first one in sixty years with no mechanical de-sugar-ing. There is no compiler to read, no guarantee, nothing to check the sweetness against except your own understanding of what should have come out.

Syntactic salt is a construct that makes bad code harder to write. Syntactic saccharin is sweetness with nothing underneath. Well, nuch of the generated code that we read is saccharin. It runs, it looks like the real thing, and the variables might as well be foo and bar. Telling the difference means knowing what the thing dissolves into, which is the knowledge everyone assumes is now free.

A local uncle once handed me a broken IBM laptop belonging to a church, and I got it back to a usable state by reloading a fresh AUTOEXEC.BAT. I did not understand much. I understood one layer below the failure, and that was enough. Now, AI raises the ceiling on what we can produce.

We have always written in sugar and have always made things easier for our successors. The problem is the cargo cult: fluent in the sweet layer, no way down, trusting an expansion nobody can verify.

  1. P. J. Landin, The Mechanical Evaluation of Expressions, appeared in The Computer Journal, Volume 6, Issue 4, January 1964. ↩

entry.title: 10x is Easier Than 2x
entry.content:
Ten times the result, and less work than doubling. I read 10x Is Easier Than 2x by Dan Sullivan and Benjamin Hardy1 expecting motivational multipliers but got something of an argument about subtraction.

You can reach 2x by doing more of what you already do. More clients, more hours, more of the same. It is a volume problem, and effort solves volume problems. That is why 2x is exhausting rather than difficult.

10x will not yield to volume. Nothing you are currently doing, done harder, gets you there. The only route left is to work out which fifth of your work produces nearly all of the result, and to let the other four fifths go.

This book is the Pareto Principle2, applied over and over. Each jump keeps the 20% and discards the rest, and the 20% you kept becomes the entire field for the next round. The book’s favorite image is Michelangelo in front of a block of marble, removing everything that is not the statue.

“How do we grow 20% next year” returns a list of things you are already doing with slightly larger figures beside them. “What would have to be true for this to be ten times bigger” returns a different list, and most of it is things you would have to stop.

This is why the honest answer to “can we also do X” is so often no. Not because X is bad, but because the list is the product.

I have watched this play out in product reviews for years. Ask a team to improve a feature and they will polish it. Ask them what the product would look like if it did a tenth as much and mattered ten times more, and the meeting stops being about the feature and becomes an argument about what the product is for.

Be warned; this is a Strategic Coach book, and it carries the house vocabulary. Unique Ability, Who Not How, the Gap, and the Gain. Each idea arrives with its capital letters and a client testimonial attached, and if you have read Sullivan’s earlier books you will meet all of them again here, at length.

The examples are also, every one of them, people who made it. Nobody in these pages drops eighty percent of their clients and ends up worse off, which is not the same as nobody ever having done so. Every book in this genre has a survivorship problem.

And “easier” is carrying a great deal of weight in that title. 10x is not easier. It is differently hard, over a much smaller surface, with far more variance. What the book means is that 10x is easier to see, because the goal is so far out of reach that it eliminates most of your options for you.

There is a freedom being assumed, too. Letting go of most of your clients is a founder’s move, and it takes runway, or a partner, or twenty years of reputation to fall back on. From inside a job, with a mortgage, the advice needs translating before it can be used.

Two Things

The first is that constraints clarify. A target you cannot reach by working harder forces you to say out loud what you actually believe produces the result. Most of us have never had to say it out loud.

The second is that subtraction is a decision, and it is the one nobody schedules. We plan what to add every quarter. I have sat in very few meetings called to decide what to stop.

You can read this one inspectionally3 in an afternoon and lose nothing. The argument is in the first third; the rest is the same argument with more customers in it.

  1. Dan Sullivan founded Strategic Coach, the entrepreneur coaching program, with Babs Smith in 1989, and most of the book’s vocabulary is the program’s. Benjamin Hardy is an organizational psychologist and the writer of the pair. This is their third together, after Who Not How in 2020 and The Gap and the Gain in 2021. ↩

  2. The Pareto principle holds that roughly 80% of the outcomes come from 20% of the causes. It is named for Vilfredo Pareto, who noticed in 1896 that about twenty percent of Italians owned about eighty percent of the land. Pareto observed the distribution. He did not suggest you apply it to yourself, recursively, forever. ↩

  3. Systematic skimming, and a real skill rather than cheating. See How to Read a Book. ↩

entry.title: User Experience of Nomenclature
entry.content:
“You’ve got to start with the customer experience and work backwards to the technology.”

That quote is the clichéd but a true one from Steve Jobs in his closing Q&A in the Apple’s Worldwide Developers Conference in 1997.

This applies even to the Nomenclatures1 that we use in email subjects, meeting titles, and even files & folder names.

I’ve seen so many meeting invites titled, “discussion”, “meeting”, “decision-making for tech stack”, etc. Of course, the most common offenders are emails that have subjects sent by people without imagination, “Pick your brain”, “Is Friday OK”, “Beta Test”, etc.

A descriptive email subject is a good indicator of what the content should be, “CompanyName › Beta Invitation”, “Introduction: PersonOne ‹› PersonTwo”, etc. are fantastic examples of good ones.

Meeting invites titled, “Intro: Brajeshwar ‹› PersonBeingIntroduced” is way easier to parse fast and still get the gist of the details. Even if I’m the one inviting the PersonBeingIntroduced because when they sees the subject/title in their calendar, they know who they are meeting without reading the full content of the meeting invite. Similarly, something in the lines of, “CompanyName › Project Kickstart” would be enough to tell me everything about that meeting.

I’m going to tell you a story from the early days of my career. A back-end developer and I used to build many software, and websites for clinics, and physicians. This was the time when websites were built on TABLES2. Assets in them were separate .gif, .png, or .jpg files.

For instance, to name all types of arrows, I’d used a reverse but logical naming convention, such as, arrow-left, arrow-right, arrow-up, arrow-down instead of the way we say, left-arrow or right-arrow. This was the early 2000s. After over a decade, I met the team maintaining the website later in the 2010s, and the first thing the team leader reminded me was the standard of names, files, and folder organization in the project. It made it easy for the team to navigate, know where things are likely to be, and they are sort-able easily into the right categories, groups, etc. Personally, it was a very proud moment.

We all have gone through the final_final filenames. That website_comp_v4.2_final_final_final_final_of_the_fina.psd was never the final one.

While dealing with files, if you’d rather not deal with categories/tags for folders, use international standard dates to start the name your files and folders, YYYY-MM-DD or YYYYMMDD. Something like;

  • 2007-07-07-wedding-bride-with-parents.jpg
  • 2008-12-11-kid-first-day.jpg etc.

Of course, if the file or folder are of a specific item/object but time if the variant, then it is better to have;

  • brajeshwar-profile-2010.jpg
  • brajeshwar-profile-2020.jpg
  • brajeshwar-profile-2026.jpg etc.

Now, naming roads such as Hollywood Boulevard, MG Road makes sense as they are descriptive and tells you where they are. Unfortunately, this is not so for files, folders, groups, categories on your devices. Don’t name your files like invoice-file.pdf, or Discussion Folder, or named your team/group as design-team or AI-group.

Be descriptive, not verbose.

Try to be descriptive, be helpful, and be consistent.

  1. Nomenclature is a system of names or terms, along with the rules for forming those terms within a particular field of art or science. Its principles range from the loose conventions of everyday speech to internationally agreed rules governing specialist terminology in scientific and other disciplines. Where onomastics studies names themselves, nomenclature is concerned more with the conventions by which names get made. ↩

  2. The <table> HTML element represents tabular data—that is, information presented in a two-dimensional table comprised of rows and columns of cells containing data. ↩
entry.summary: “You’ve got to start with the customer experience and work backwards to the technology.”

entry.title: How to Read a Book
entry.content:
Or, what reading since the 1990s did not teach me.

After decades of reading books, I have decided to finally learn How to Read a Book. There is a particular kind of embarrassment in that sentence, and I have made my peace with it.

Mortimer J. Adler published it in 1940. He revised it in 1972 with Charles Van Doren1, and that is the edition I read, and most likely the one you have too. It is not a book about loving books. It is closer to a manual, written by a man who believed reading is a skill, that most adults quietly stopped learning it somewhere around the sixth grade, and that this was worth being blunt about.

He splits reading into four levels, each one folded into the next.

Elementary is what school gave you. What does the sentence say? Most of us stopped here and have been coasting ever since.

Inspectional is reading on a budget. Systematic skimming (the table of contents, the index, the preface, a paragraph here and there) to answer one question: what kind of book is this, and does it deserve more of my life? Adler is emphatic that this is a real skill and not cheating.

Analytical is the heart of the book and most of its pages. You classify the book, work out its structure, come to terms with the author2, which means agreeing on what his words mean before you argue with them, and only then judge it. The rule I keep returning to is his one about disagreement: you must be able to say “I understand” before you are allowed to say “I agree,” “I disagree,” or “I suspend judgment.”

Syntopical is reading many books on one subject and building an understanding that sits in none of them individually. It is the hardest, and it is the one that actually changes how you think.

So, What Now?

Well, the book is kind of a slog. There is a real irony in a book about reading being this hard to finish. It is repetitive, fond of its own taxonomy, and the 137-title reading list at the back3 is Homer-to-Solzhenitsyn Western canon in a way that has aged into a period piece.

Of course, the ideas are what you take away from the book. Inspectional reading gave me permission to stop apologizing for skimming. “Come to terms with the author” has made me a better arguer and a much slower one.

What follows is my own take: the whys, and some of the hows, gathered over years of reading and of stealing good ideas from the Internet.

Why Read?

  1. Reading well will deepen your appreciation of literature; you’ll gain new experiences and enrich your knowledge of the world and other people.
  2. Reading well requires noticing details, reflecting on them and questioning them.
  3. One key to reading well and pleasurably is to slow down, take your time and read deliberatively.
  4. Re-reading literary texts will allow you to pick up on what you missed the first time around and deepen your reading pleasure.
  5. Reading aloud, whether a sentence or an entire page, will help you notice more about a writer’s craft and art, especially how the tone and texture complement the meaning.

How to read books the right way

  1. Pick up multiple books (physical, digital, or audio) from the same topic or category to go deeper. This is Adler’s syntopical reading, and you can start it without his permission.
  2. It is OK not to finish a book you don’t like.
  3. Some books are more flexible and might not be read linearly. It does depend on the topic of the book you’re reading. It’s okay to pick up chapters if the book is meant to be a collection of answers to unrelated topics.
  4. Write notes, highlight them, or stick tiny stickies on pages (for physical books).
  5. You can speed-read4 parts and sections that might not be useful to remember.
  6. While reading you might come across topics you don’t know much about. While you’re still finishing the book, read a brief summary to get through the current content. Write them down separately to research more later.
  7. Try to write a summary after you’ve read the whole book.
  8. Find your format/style or mix them up: digital, physical, audio.

Tips

Here are a few personal tips that worked for me while trying to read and learn the contents of books and get the best out of them. This will help you overcome the habit of Tsundoku5.

  • Read reviews, from multiple sources, of a book and try to know a general idea of the content and idea of that book.
  • Or listen to audio books at about 1.2x speed. You can use whatever you are comfortable with: a headphone, or in your car.
  • Once you have either read the reviews or heard the audio book, decide if you want to read the book or not. When you do read it, either physical or digital, but now you know which part to browse and which part to concentrate on.

That last one is inspectional reading wearing a disguise, which I did not know until I read Adler. I had spent years arriving at a worse version of a method somebody wrote down before my parents were born. That is either humbling or reassuring, and most days I take it as both.

  1. Charles Van Doren is a strange co-author for this particular book. In 1957 he won $129,000 on the NBC quiz show Twenty-One and made the cover of Time, and in November 1959 he told a Congressional subcommittee that he had been given the questions and answers in advance. “I was involved, deeply involved, in a deception.” He joined Encyclopædia Britannica the same year, worked alongside Adler for the next two decades, and thirteen years after the confession co-wrote the standard book on reading honestly. ↩

  2. “Coming to terms” is Adler’s pun and his fifth rule of analytical reading. A term, for him, is not a word but a word used with a single unambiguous meaning. When the writer and the reader are using the important words the same way, they have come to terms, in both senses. ↩

  3. The list is the short version of Great Books of the Western World, the 54-volume set Adler edited with Robert Hutchins in 1952. Its first two volumes are the Syntopicon, an index not of words but of 102 ideas, cross-referencing every mention of each one across the whole set. It took eight years and a staff of indexers, and it is the most literal thing anyone has ever built for syntopical reading. ↩

  4. Speed Reading is the technique of chunking and minimizing subvocalization. The many available speed-reading training programs may utilize books, videos, software, and seminars. There is little scientific evidence regarding speed reading, and as a result its value seems uncertain. ↩

  5. Tsundoku (Japanese: 積ん読) is the art of buying books and never reading them. ↩
entry.summary: Or, what reading since the 1990s did not teach me.

entry.title: Acronyms Ad Absurdum
entry.content:
Daniel’s Acronym Fatigue Series started this train of thought, and everything came flashing back that I thought I would write it out.

It all started, small, with a harmless ASAP, and then a cheeky FYI. Sometimes, I remember pausing in the middle of meetings and pondering, “Let’s double-click on the OKRs before we boil the ocean on this NPS dip,” and nodded along.

Nobody disagrees with you in a meeting these days; they “push back to build alignment,” which is corporate for “no, and I will smile while saying it.” Somewhere a UX researcher is drowning a perfectly good sentence like “people don’t like this button” under a life vest made entirely of consonants: CTR, CSAT, NPS, and, if the deck is feeling ambitious, a lone, defiant ROI.

The acronyms I can just about live with these days; they’re at least honest about being shortcuts. It’s the phrases & jargons that have quietly colonized my brain that worry me. “Let’s take this offline” is a sentence that has never once resulted in an offline conversation, only a calendar invite for Thursday that slides into “next sprint,” the corporate underworld where unresolved decisions go to reincarnate as new tickets.

“Low-hanging fruit,” as if anyone in the history of quarterly planning has ever picked it, rather than just pointed at it approvingly in a slide and moved on to slide thirteen. “We need to operationalize the learnings” is just “we should probably write this down.”

One of my favorites is “leverage synergies,” a phrase so devoid of content it should officially require a laugh track. Somewhere, in an alternate universe with better labor laws, two departments are simply working together, and nobody had to invent a portmanteau1 of “energy” and “lever” to describe it.

Ah! And then there is the “North Star Metric.” We didn’t need six thousand years of celestial navigation vocabulary to say “the number we’re staring at in the dashboard until it goes up.” Sailors used actual stars to avoid actual death. We are using them to avoid saying, “We don’t really know if this feature worked.”

The tell, always, is that the jargon shows up hardest exactly where the thinking is thinnest. Nobody needs a TLA (three-letter acronym; we even made an acronym for that, which should honestly disqualify the entire species from further language privileges) to say “the database is slow.” But tell a room, “We’re facing latency-driven churn risk impacting our activation funnel,” and suddenly you sound like someone who deserves a promotion instead of someone who forgot to add an index.

I’m not against efficiency. Truly. Some acronyms earn their keep; HTTP didn’t ruin anyone’s day. But most corporate jargon isn’t compression; they are costumes. It doesn’t make the idea smaller and faster. It makes the absence of an idea harder to notice.

So, can we circle back on plain English? Put it on the roadmap. And, I’ll own the action item.

  1. Portmanteau is a word formed by merging the sounds and meanings of two different words, as chortle, from chuckle and snort. ↩
entry.summary: Daniel’s Acronym Fatigue Series started this train of thought, and everything came flashing back that I thought I would write it out.

entry.title: You are brajeshwar.com?
entry.content:
In 2010-2011, I was in Mountain View while undergoing an entrepreneurship course at the Founder Institute. Besides the usual coffee and lunch places, I frequented Hacker Dojo. I remember that my friends and I even did some presentations, and participated in a few Hackathons there.

On a fateful rainy evening, as usual, I was slouched on my Laptop on one of the common desk at Hacker Dojo. Someone approached me and asked, “You are brajeshwar.com, right?” (or something in that line). We chatted a bit and I was super happy about that. I could no longer recollect who that was.

It was also at this time that I registered the domain hackathon.co (Feb 14, 2011) to run hackathons and write about it. I later sold the domain and the content for a good sum within few months of its registration and launch.
